question.prompt:
Three one-inch squares are placed with their bases on a line. The center square is lifted out and rotated \(45^\circ,\) as shown. Then it is centered and lowered into its original location until it touches both of the adjoining squares. How many inches is the point \(B\) from the line on which the bases of the original squares were placed?

[Figure 1](figures/2005_AMC_10A_Q19_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The useful point to locate first is the lowest vertex of the rotated square. Call it \(V\). Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be the inner upper corners of the fixed squares, where contact occurs, and let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(PQ\).

Removing the middle unit square leaves a gap \(1\) inch wide. Thus \(PQ=1\), and \(P\), \(Q\), and \(M\) are all \(1\) inch above the baseline. Because the rotated square is centered, its vertical diagonal passes through \(M\), so \(PM=1/2\).

The lower edges of the rotated square make \(45^\circ\) angles with the horizontal. Consequently, \(PMV\) is a right triangle with two \(45^\circ\) angles, so its legs are equal:
\[
MV=PM=\frac12.
\]
Therefore \(V\) is \(1-1/2=1/2\) inch above the baseline. The contact lies on each unit edge because \(PV=\sqrt{(1/2)^2+(1/2)^2}=1/\sqrt2<1\).

Rotation preserves the square's side lengths. Its diagonal, from \(V\) to the top vertex \(B\), is vertical and has length
\[
VB=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2
\]
by the Pythagorean theorem. Adding this to the height of \(V\), the distance from \(B\) to the horizontal baseline is
\[
\boxed{\sqrt2+\frac12}\text{ inches},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
solutions.title: Locate the bottom vertex
